title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator Suite for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We designed, preregistered, and executed a reproducible synthetic benchmark plus a deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM configuration generator on operational intent→configuration tasks. The preregistered paired design used N=300 tasks across four intent categories (75 per cluster) and declared model gpt-5-mini; the deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). Outcomes were binary per task (validator pass/fail). Results: baseline (single‑pass) 299/300 passes, guarded (GVR) 300/300 passes; paired contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0033333333333332993; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered hypothesis that GVR materially increases pass rate (target effect 0.10 with planned ≈80% power at N=300) was not supported. We provide (and reference) the sealed preregistration (ac-2026-003-prereg-v1), execution manifest, raw responses, and analysis artifacts. We interpret the outcome as driven by a ceiling effect under the chosen synthetic tasks and snapshot validator semantics, discuss construct and external validity limits, and release the benchmark and artifacts for community extension.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are widely proposed to automate NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation and change planning. Prior studies report that naive LLM outputs can contain syntax, topology, or semantic errors and that combining generation with deterministic validators and localized repair can reduce such errors. However, the community lacks a standardized, machine‑checkable benchmark that couples realistic (synthetic) intent tasks, formalized validator semantics, and a sealed confirmatory protocol for paired comparisons. We therefore preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (ac-2026-003-prereg-v1) to ask: Can a standardized synthetic task set and deterministic validator reveal a material per‑task correctness advantage for a GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass LLM under fixed seeds and execution budget? Our principal contribution is (1) the benchmark generator and validator suite, (2) a sealed preregistered paired experiment (N=300) comparing GVR to single‑pass generation with gpt-5-mini, and (3) the archived execution and analysis artifacts that document a near‑ceiling outcome and lessons for benchmark design.
sections.related_work: Surveys and reviews summarize rapid growth in LLM applications for NetOps and identify failure modes and evaluation gaps [Long et al., 2025; Hong et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2024]. Prior technical work shows LLMs can synthesize router configurations but often require verifier assistance to avoid misconfigurations [Mondal et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2024]. CAIP demonstrated context‑aware iterative prompting to detect/correct router misconfigurations [Jiang et al., 2024]. Security research highlights prompt injection and adversarial risks that are relevant to operational NetOps workflows [Shen et al., 2024]. These prior findings motivated a preregistered, artifact‑grounded confirmatory comparison focused on operationally expressed, machine‑checkable correctness rather than only language‑level fidelity.
sections.methodology: Preregistration. The study plan (ac-2026-003-prereg-v1; preregistration SHA‑256: a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765) predeclared the primary hypothesis H1: the GVR pipeline yields a higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass LLM on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). The design is paired (each task shares the same initial generation candidate) with maximum_model_calls=600 and maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1. Task bank. A deterministic synthetic task generator produced 300 intent→configuration tasks spanning four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 tasks per cluster). Each task encodes an initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, and workflow_policies (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, minimum_active_in_groups). Model and orchestration. Declared model: gpt-5-mini. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter implemented both the baseline single‑pass generation (shared initial candidate) and the guarded GVR pipeline (generate→validator→at most one automated repair). Validator specification (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). The validator (v5.0) performed deterministic, snapshot (stateless) machine‑checkable validation under the scoring rule labeled "full_intent_constraint_validation." Operationally, the validator: (a) parses generated commands into normalized command tokens and normalizes ordering where semantically permitted; (b) compares the normalized configuration to the task’s expected_final_state and required_sequence; (c) enforces declared workflow_policies including must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, and minimum_active_in_groups; (d) enforces "preserve_unspecified_state" when requested; (e) reports structured diagnostics (validator_id, validator_version, normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes, violation_count, and a boolean valid flag); and (f) emits a binary score where score=1 with score_reason_code=VALID_CONFIGURATION indicates the generated configuration satisfied all required constraints. The scoring rule and these fields are visible in the archived per‑task scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/*.json). Analysis plan. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The predeclared primary test was an exact McNemar two‑sided test on the paired binary outcomes. A paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI was computed with 10,000 resamples (seed 1729). Missingness and exclusions. Predeclared exclusion rules removed items with ambiguous specifications or contamination; the run recorded no such exclusions and completed the planned N=300 pairs. Reproducibility. Seeds, provider traces, model configuration, and all outputs were archived; actual model_calls_used and execution accounting are recorded in the execution manifest.
sections.results: Execution. The confirmatory run completed per the preregistered plan: completed_pair_count = 300; model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial generation calls + 1 repair call); failed_episode_count = 0. Primary outcomes. Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (baseline_success_rate = 0.9966666666666667). Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). Paired contingency (guarded,baseline): n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729): [0.00, 0.01]. The full condition summary and contingency table are archived (analysis/condition_summary.csv and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) and were the direct inputs to the confirmatory executor. Exploratory analyses. Planned exploratory diagnostics (failure‑mode clustering, per‑cluster summaries, and inter‑run reproducibility metrics) were executed; only one discordant pair was observed (n10=1), which prevents meaningful clustering or subgroup inference. Representative scoring examples are provided in execution/scoring/*.json and show validator fields such as normalized_configuration, required_command_count, and validator version (deterministic_netops_validator_v5 v5.0).
sections.discussion: Interpretation and power reconciliation. The preregistration power calculation targeted detection of a 0.10 absolute paired difference with N=300 (≈80% power under conservative discordance assumptions). The observed baseline success rate (299/300 ≈ 0.9967) produces a strong ceiling effect: with baseline ≈99.7% there is effectively no headroom to detect a 0.10 improvement, and the observed paired difference (0.00333) is far smaller than the preregistered target. Consequently, the preregistered sensitivity assumptions do not apply to the observed outcome distribution; the study thus provides a valid negative result under the chosen task and validator semantics but cannot adjudicate whether GVR would outperform single‑pass generation on substantially harder or more stateful tasks. Construct validity and limitations of the validator. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot, task‑declared workflow_policies and required sequences; it does not simulate temporal in‑flight dynamics, vendor execution idiosyncrasies, or performance impacts. Hence a configuration that passes this validator may still be operationally risky in a live heterogeneous network. External validity. Tasks were synthetically generated (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and thus do not exhaust production heterogeneity. Operational implication. Near‑ceiling results under these validator semantics motivate community efforts to (a) extend benchmarks to richer, stateful validators (temporal simulation or emulation), (b) expand task difficulty and heterogeneity, and (c) run multi‑model, multi‑vendor comparisons. The archived bundle provides the substrate to pursue these extensions.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a reproducible synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator suite and ran a paired confirmatory comparison of a GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Both methods achieved near‑perfect validator pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300); the preregistered primary hypothesis that GVR materially improves pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported on this task set. The result highlights the central role of benchmark and validator design: ceiling effects and narrow validator construct semantics can mask method differences. We release the task generator, deterministic validator specification (archived artifacts), raw outputs, and analysis artifacts to enable community extensions (harder tasks, stateful validators, multi‑model evaluations) that can better reveal where GVR pipelines provide measurable operational value.

disclosure_statement: This study followed the sealed preregistration ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 (preregistration SHA‑256: a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765) and used archived execution and analysis artifacts. Declared model: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). Orchestration/adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 implementing both the baseline single‑pass generation (shared initial candidate) and the guarded generate–validate–repair pipeline. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version v5.0) implementing the scoring rule labeled "full_intent_constraint_validation" (validator semantics summarized in Methodology; per‑task scorer outputs are archived under execution/scoring/*.json). Initial master prompt: archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human role and autonomy: a human Research Director selected the topic family and provided pre‑lock constraints; after the autonomy lock the autonomous pipeline performed literature synthesis, study selection, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and revision. No manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Execution accounting: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, completed_pair_count = 300, model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial + 1 repair). No post‑preregistration design changes or manual restarts were performed to influence scientific outcomes; execution manifest records zero failed episodes. All generated tasks, provider traces, validator outputs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the execution bundle with recorded artifact hashes; the execution manifest and analysis artifacts are the authoritative provenance record for the empirical claims in this paper.
limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot, task‑declared workflow_policies and required sequences but does not model temporal in‑flight dynamics, vendor execution idiosyncrasies, or traffic/performance impacts.

External validity: synthetic tasks (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) do not capture full production heterogeneity; results do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) limit sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain the confirmatory inference regarding practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further multi‑model experiments.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred, leaving planned exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing exact hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider conditions recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and the execution manifest.
